strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: efficiently combining newly internalized knowledge with reusable reasoning or tool-use behavior. The proposed residual-vector composition is simple, computationally attractive at target adaptation time, and clearly described.

The empirical scope is broader than a single benchmark, covering closed-book SQuAD, long-document LooGLE, and agentic ToolBench tasks. PaST shows sizable improvements over its matched target-SFT baseline, including +17.2 points on single-passage SQuAD, +8.0 on LooGLE, and +10.3 average tool-use success.

The ToolBench experiment provides useful evidence of cross-category transfer: the skill vector is learned only on Movies and improves all 20 evaluated target categories. The post-hoc versus pre-injection and sequential-fine-tuning comparison also supports the chosen composition order.

The appendices document many implementation details, including prompts, data splits, optimization hyperparameters, reward definitions, and simulator instructions. The iterative-refinement ablation controls the total data and optimization budget.
The paper is relevant to computational linguistics, generally clear, and candid about its restriction to Qwen2.5-7B models and a fixed vector coefficient.
weaknesses: The central claim that SFT and RL occupy disentangled subspaces is not established. Near-zero cosine similarity between two extremely high-dimensional update matrices is expected even for unrelated random vectors. The SFT-SFT control is useful but insufficient: it provides no random-vector, shuffled-label, independent-run, or norm-matched controls; no uncertainty; and appears to use only one model and a very small LooGLE sample. Observing two nearly orthogonal update directions does not establish subspace disentanglement or domain-independent skill.

The theoretical argument overclaims a proof. LayerNorm does not imply zero-centered isotropic, independent sub-Gaussian activations; Frobenius orthogonality only yields zero expected signal inner product under the assumed covariance and does not ensure low interference for individual inputs. The stated concentration reasoning does not establish the required relative bound merely because dimension is large. Consequently, it cannot justify claims that subtraction removes domain content or that downstream components route the signals independently.

The experiments do not cleanly isolate an RL-derived skill. PaST receives substantial additional supervision and compute: labeled or synthetic source QA, 10–15 epochs of GRPO with GPT-4.1 rewards, or PPO trajectories and an API simulator. The principal baselines generally receive only target SFT, while SEAL numbers are imported from prior work. Missing controls include an equally trained SFT task vector, a norm-matched random vector, shuffled-reward RL, supervised training on the same source trajectories, Reasoning Vectors or other task-vector methods, and target-domain RL as an upper bound. Thus, gains could reflect transferred task/format behavior or extra supervision rather than the claimed knowledge-manipulation skill.

The strongest SQuAD comparison is not resource matched: PaST uses up to 100 source documents and their QA pairs plus a proprietary reward model, whereas the reported SEAL and synthetic-SFT baselines do not receive equivalent auxiliary training. Moreover, SQuAD-to-SQuAD transfer demonstrates new-document transfer within the same dataset and task, not broad domain-agnostic transfer.

Evaluation reliability is underdeveloped. SQuAD and LooGLE accuracy relies entirely on GPT-4.1 judgments without human validation or judge-agreement analysis. ToolBench uses both a GPT-4o-mini simulator and GPT-4.1 success judge, creating possible simulator/judge artifacts. Several tool categories contain only 3–5 queries; despite three generations, no confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or per-seed results are reported.

The reported LooGLE results vary substantially by evaluation slice: Table 2 reports 30.1 versus 38.1 over 50 documents, while the first-10-document ablations report 32.9 versus 44.6. The manuscript explains the different subset but does not report question counts, uncertainty, or consistent full-test ablations, limiting comparability and confidence.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the detailed appendix. No code, trained vectors, generated training data, model outputs, or exact random seeds are supplied, and core training and evaluation depend on mutable proprietary GPT-4.1/GPT-4o-mini services. Some protocol details needed to reproduce Table 1 and the vector injection across LoRA versus full-fine-tuning regimes are unclear.

Overall, the empirical pattern is promising, but the causal and theoretical claims substantially exceed the evidence. Stronger matched controls, statistically supported evaluations, and a corrected or substantially weakened orthogonality argument are needed before the work clearly meets the soundness bar for Findings.

strengths: The proposed parameter-arithmetic method is simple, computationally practical at target-adaptation time, and directly relevant to continual knowledge adaptation in NLP.

The manuscript evaluates one underlying model family across three settings—closed-book SQuAD, long-document LooGLE, and tool use—and reports sizable gains over matched target-SFT baselines, including gains across all 20 ToolBench target categories.
Useful implementation details are supplied for SFT, GRPO/PPO, prompts, data splits, and reward design. The iterative-refinement and injection-stage ablations are informative preliminary analyses.

The paper recognizes closely related task-arithmetic and Reasoning Vector work and presents its intended contribution as applying RL residual transfer specifically to knowledge adaptation. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/1536ac16bcb44af0a01b0e61aac940a0/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central interpretation is not established. The residual between an RL model and its SFT initialization is labeled a domain-agnostic skill vector, but RL is performed on document-specific QA or tool trajectories, so the residual can contain source facts, answer-format behavior, judge-specific adaptations, and other changes. Cross-domain gains show useful transfer, but do not demonstrate the claimed knowledge/skill decomposition. Necessary controls include RL–RL similarities across domains, shuffled-reward or random-vector controls, SFT-derived vectors, matched-norm perturbations, and direct tests of retained source information.

The claimed theoretical proof is unsound. LayerNorm does not justify isotropic, independent, sub-Gaussian activations; zero expected inner product does not imply functional independence or absence of destructive interference; and the stated Hanson–Wright argument incorrectly says concentration necessarily improves with dimension even while its bound depends on norms that may grow with dimension. Orthogonality of two update matrices also does not show that downstream components route their signals separately. These results should be reframed as a limited empirical observation rather than a proof of disentanglement.

The empirical comparisons are insufficient for the broad claims. LooGLE is compared only with the authors' SFT baseline, without stronger knowledge-incorporation methods, long-context/RAG approaches, or target-domain RL as an upper bound. ToolBench likewise lacks target-RL and task-vector controls. Consequently, it is unclear whether PaST transfers knowledge-manipulation ability specifically, generic ReAct/format-following behavior, or merely a favorable parameter perturbation.

Evaluation uncertainty is inadequately handled. LooGLE and ToolBench use three stochastic generations rather than independent training and data-selection seeds. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported. Many ToolBench categories contain only 3–15 queries, making category-level gains such as 0% to 16.7% highly unstable; macro-averaging these small categories can exaggerate evidence. SQuAD results also lack variance despite reliance on stochastic training and an LLM judge.

ToolBench validity is uncertain because both execution and success are mediated by proprietary models: GPT-4o-mini simulates APIs and GPT-4.1 judges trajectories. The simulator is not validated against real APIs or the StableToolBench execution environment, and judge agreement is not measured. Reward training also uses GPT-4.1, so evaluation with the same model family risks reward/evaluator coupling.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive appendix. The exact SQuAD source document identities, random seeds, generated datasets, checkpoint artifacts, filtering code, and sampling settings are not fully specified or released; some settings defer to SEAL. Reproduction also requires proprietary GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o-mini. There are smaller reporting inconsistencies, including LooGLE results of 38.1 on 50 documents versus 44.6 in ablations on 10 documents without consistently foregrounding the changed evaluation subset, and a description of SFT data that alternates between two components and a three-component mixture.

The novelty relative to established task-vector arithmetic and the cited Reasoning Vectors method is limited. The main distinction is the knowledge-adaptation application and iterative extraction procedure, but the paper does not isolate the latter convincingly enough to establish a substantial new technical contribution.

Overall, the method is promising and the reported gains warrant further investigation, but the central causal and theoretical claims substantially exceed the evidence. Establishing what the residual contains, adding competitive and causal controls, validating evaluation reliability, and reporting seeded uncertainty constitute important revisions; therefore the work is not yet sound enough for Findings.

strengths: PaST is a simple and practically appealing use of task-vector arithmetic: an RL-induced parameter residual is extracted on source data and added after target-domain SFT, avoiding target-side RL.

The empirical results are consistently positive across three settings. Reported gains include +17.2 points over matched SFT on single-passage SQuAD, +8.0 points on LooGLE, and +10.3 average success-rate points across 20 RL-unseen ToolBench categories.

The evaluation spans closed-book factual recall, long-document knowledge incorporation, and multi-turn tool use. The improvement in every evaluated ToolBench target category is particularly encouraging evidence of positive transfer.

Ablations compare one- and two-round extraction, equal-budget single-round training, sequential fine-tuning, pre-injection, and post-hoc injection. These results support the specific iterative, post-hoc design rather than merely showing that additional training helps.

The paper is clearly motivated and generally well organized. Appendices provide prompts, data construction procedures, reward definitions, hardware, and extensive SFT/RL hyperparameters, supporting partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim that SFT and RL updates occupy semantically disentangled knowledge and skill subspaces is not established. Near-zero cosine similarity is common for high-dimensional updates, and a single SFT–SFT control does not rule out alternatives such as optimizer, objective, scale, or data differences. Random-vector, RL–RL, shuffled-reward, matched-objective, and multiple-seed controls are needed.

The theoretical argument overstates what follows from orthogonality. It depends on activations being isotropic and independently sub-Gaussian—properties not implied by LayerNorm—and Frobenius orthogonality only gives zero expected signal overlap under those assumptions. The stated concentration conclusion does not follow merely because dimensionality is large; the cited bound also depends on the relevant matrix norms. Thus it does not prove functional independence or absence of interference.

The evidence supports task-specific transfer across documents or categories, not a broadly domain-agnostic reasoning skill. Separate vectors are trained for SQuAD, LooGLE, and ToolBench, and source and target data retain the same benchmark, task format, reward, and evaluation protocol. No transfer across tasks, datasets, or model families is demonstrated.

Several gains are insufficiently quantified statistically. The paper reports three stochastic generation runs but no training-seed variation, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Many ToolBench categories contain only 3–15 test queries, making per-category rates unstable, while the average pools heterogeneous category sizes without uncertainty.

Evaluation relies heavily on proprietary GPT-4.1 judges and, for ToolBench, a GPT-4o-mini simulator. Judge agreement with humans, sensitivity to judge choice, simulator fidelity, and failure rates are not reported. Consequently, the experiments do not establish whether the tool-use gains persist with real APIs or independent evaluation.

The baseline coverage is limited, especially for tool use: PaST is primarily compared with target SFT, without target-domain RL as an oracle, source-RL transfer without subtraction, random or norm-matched vectors, SFT-derived vectors, or established tool-learning alternatives. These controls are important for attributing improvements specifically to transferable RL skill.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite detailed appendices: no code, generated datasets, checkpoints, skill vectors, exact proprietary-model versions, or API settings are provided. Some reporting is also inconsistent or ambiguous, such as the markedly different LooGLE values in the main table and ablations and the unclear evaluation subset for Table 3.

Overall, the method and results are promising, but the paper currently interprets useful empirical parameter transfer as proof of knowledge–skill disentanglement. The missing controls, weak statistical support, and questionable theoretical justification leave the Findings case unresolved rather than clearly positive.

strengths: The reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/abf2e84dd6cd4a668d1b69a9aa3112a6/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important NLP problem: efficiently enabling models to use newly internalized knowledge without rerunning reinforcement learning for every target domain. The proposed post-hoc task-vector composition is simple and practically appealing.

The reported improvements are substantial and fairly consistent: PaST improves closed-book SQuAD and LooGLE accuracy, and raises average StableToolBench success from 21.9% to 32.2% across all 20 target categories.

The paper includes useful ablations of iterative refinement, injection order, and target-domain RL budgets. The comparison among sequential fine-tuning, pre-injection, and post-hoc composition provides concrete evidence that the proposed composition order matters.

The empirical scope spans short-form QA, long-document parametric retrieval, and multi-step tool use. Appendices provide many prompts, training hyperparameters, dataset splits, reward definitions, and illustrative trajectories.
The presentation is generally clear, and the paper appropriately discusses the closely related Reasoning Vectors approach rather than presenting task-vector transfer as wholly unprecedented.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is substantially overstated. Frobenius orthogonality of two weight-update matrices, combined with an assumed isotropic activation distribution, only gives a near-zero expected unnormalized signal inner product. It does not prove statistical independence, non-interference, distinct routing by later layers, or preservation of behavior after nonlinear propagation through an entire transformer. LayerNorm does not establish independent isotropic activation coordinates. Moreover, the Hanson-Wright inequality as presented does not automatically provide stronger concentration merely because the model dimension is large; the necessary normalization and norm/effective-rank conditions are not established. Thus Appendix D is not a proof of functional disentanglement.

The cosine-similarity evidence is insufficient to establish that SFT and RL occupy meaningfully disentangled subspaces. Near-zero cosine is expected for many unrelated vectors in extremely high-dimensional spaces, while the same-modality controls are themselves only about 0.03. Averaging cosine values over modules can conceal substantial localized alignment or interference. The paper lacks random-update null distributions, seed variability, update-norm analysis, principal-angle/SVD subspace analysis, and activation- or function-level interference measurements. Orthogonality also does not by itself imply that the residual specifically encodes a domain-agnostic skill.

Key controls and comparisons are missing. Despite identifying Reasoning Vectors as the closest work, there is no direct empirical comparison. The experiments also lack matched controls using an unrelated RL residual, a random or norm-matched vector, an SFT residual, or generic RL training for formatting and termination behavior. These are especially important for ToolBench, where the source RL reward explicitly teaches broadly reusable ReAct formatting, valid calls, error handling, and Finish behavior; the gains need not demonstrate a separable knowledge-manipulation faculty.

Evaluation uncertainty is underreported. SQuAD results have no variance or confidence intervals, and the LooGLE protocol's three stochastic generations are not equivalent to independent training runs despite language suggesting independent runs. Many ToolBench categories contain only 3–15 test queries, yet no uncertainty or significance analysis is supplied. Both rewards and evaluation depend on proprietary GPT-4.1, while ToolBench additionally uses GPT-4o-mini rather than real API execution; there is no human validation, alternative judge, or simulator-fidelity study.

The scope does not support several broad claims. Experiments use only Qwen2.5-7B variants; LooGLE transfers between documents from the same benchmark rather than genuinely distinct domains; ToolBench uses only Movies as the RL source; and the paper does not test sequential knowledge updates, forgetting, retention of general capabilities, or interference across repeated adaptations. Consequently, claims about continual adaptation, architecture-general dynamics, scalability, and domain-agnostic skills should be narrowed.

The efficiency comparison reports only target-side RL time and omits the amortized source RL cost, synthetic-data generation, target SFT, model-vector storage, and full model arithmetic. PaST still requires substantial target-side fine-tuning in several settings, so statements suggesting essentially cost-free adaptation are misleading without an end-to-end compute and storage accounting.

Reproducibility is mixed: the detailed appendices are valuable, but no code, checkpoints, generated training data, exact document/query lists, random seeds, or cached proprietary-model outputs are provided. Reproducing the reported numbers would therefore remain difficult and potentially costly.

Overall, the empirical results are promising enough to approach Findings, but the paper's main mechanistic justification is not valid as stated and the experiments lack decisive controls for identifying what the transferred residual represents. Correcting the theory, narrowing the claims, and adding matched baselines and statistically robust evaluation are needed for a clear positive recommendation.

strengths: PaST is a simple and potentially useful adaptation method: an RL-induced parameter residual can be extracted once and composed with target-domain SFT checkpoints without target-side RL.

The paper evaluates the approach across three meaningfully different settings—closed-book SQuAD, long-document LooGLE, and agentic ToolBench—and reports consistently positive, sometimes large, gains over matched target-SFT models.
The post-hoc versus pre-injection/sequential-training ablation, iterative-refinement study, and direct target-domain RL comparison are relevant and help characterize the method.
The appendices provide substantial implementation detail, including prompts, training curricula, hyperparameters, data splits, and reward definitions.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim is not established. Near-zero cosine similarity between two high-dimensional update vectors does not demonstrate that knowledge and skill occupy disentangled subspaces, that the RL residual is content-free, or that the two functions coexist without interference. A single scalar inner product can also hide cancellation across parameters and layers.

The theoretical argument overreaches and contains a questionable concentration claim. Layer normalization does not imply independent, isotropic, sub-Gaussian activations; orthogonality at one linear transformation does not establish functional independence through a nonlinear transformer; and growth of the matrix norm in the stated Hanson–Wright bound does not by itself make concentration around zero stronger.

The experiments show that an RL-derived delta helps, but do not isolate the proposed explanation. Missing controls include matched-norm random deltas, additional-training/SFT deltas, unrelated RL deltas, and direct comparison with the closely related Reasoning Vectors extraction method. Consequently, improvements cannot confidently be attributed to orthogonal knowledge-skill decomposition.

Statistical support is inadequate. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported. Several ToolBench categories contain only 3–5 test queries, making category-level claims such as improvement in all 20 categories unstable. The LooGLE appendix indicates that the reported three runs are stochastic generation passes rather than independent training runs, despite the main text's stronger wording.

Evaluation relies heavily on proprietary GPT-4.1 judgments and a GPT-4o-mini simulated tool environment. Judge agreement with humans, robustness to alternative judges, and actual API execution are not evaluated. This is particularly consequential for the ToolBench claims.

Some conclusions misstate the evidence. PaST does not outperform the GPT-4.1-synthetic baseline in every SQuAD regime, and the second refinement round slightly degrades CPT-200 performance. Results on the first 10 LooGLE documents also differ substantially from the 50-document evaluation, without uncertainty estimates explaining the variation.

The paper evaluates only Qwen2.5-7B variants and does not test retention of general or source-domain capabilities after full-vector addition. Thus, robustness across architectures and possible collateral degradation remain unknown.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of released code, checkpoints, generated datasets, seeds, and versioned proprietary-model outputs. Although the appendices are detailed, reproducing the complete pipeline would remain costly and partly dependent on changing closed models.

Overall, the empirical signal is promising, but the unsupported mechanistic interpretation, weak uncertainty analysis, and missing causal and prior-method controls prevent a clear Findings recommendation in the current form. A next-cycle revision could become suitable by narrowing the claims and adding rigorous controls and replicated evaluations.

strengths: PaST is a simple, practically motivated approach: an RL-induced parameter residual is extracted after source-domain SFT and added post hoc to a target-domain SFT model, avoiding target-side RL. The iterative refinement and post-hoc composition variants are clearly specified.

The empirical evidence is broad and consistently positive. Gains are reported for closed-book SQuAD, long-document LooGLE, and 20 RL-unseen ToolBench categories; the comparisons with pre-injection, sequential fine-tuning, and target-domain RL help establish the practical value of the proposed composition strategy.

The appendices provide substantial implementation detail, including data splits, prompts, training procedures, hyperparameters, reward definitions, and simulator instructions. This is considerably better documented than many large-scale RL studies.

The work is clearly relevant to NLP: it addresses continual knowledge incorporation, parametric retrieval, and tool-using language models. The paper is generally well organized, and its tables and motivating examples make the method easy to understand.

The efficiency argument is meaningful in an amortized setting: a reusable source skill vector can recover much of the measured benefit of per-document target RL without repeating expensive on-policy training for every target document.
weaknesses: The paper overstates what near-zero cosine similarity establishes. Orthogonality of two aggregate parameter-update matrices does not by itself demonstrate that one update contains knowledge and the other contains a separable, domain-agnostic skill, nor that their nonlinear network functions do not interfere. The proposed theoretical argument depends on strong, unverified isotropy and independence assumptions; LayerNorm does not guarantee them. Moreover, the Hanson-Wright discussion does not justify the claim that concentration improves merely because the dimension is large without a normalized bound and appropriate norm scaling. This should be presented as a heuristic motivation, not a proof of functional disentanglement.

Important controls are missing. The experiments do not compare directly with the closest Reasoning Vectors formulation, norm-matched SFT or random update vectors, or RL residuals learned for unrelated tasks. Such controls are needed to attribute gains specifically to transferable procedural skill rather than generic parameter perturbation, answer-format adaptation, or benchmark-specific behavior.

The claimed domain generality is only partially tested. SQuAD and LooGLE transfer between documents within the same respective benchmark, while ToolBench transfer is between categories within one dataset and simulator. All experiments use one model family at approximately one scale. Consequently, the evidence supports within-benchmark transfer much more strongly than broad domain-agnostic skill transfer.

Evaluation uncertainty is insufficiently quantified. Many ToolBench categories contain only 3–13 test queries, yet category-level gains are emphasized without confidence intervals or paired significance tests. Repeated stochastic generations on the same fixed questions are not equivalent to independent training or test samples. SQuAD and LooGLE also rely on GPT-4.1 judging without reported human validation, judge sensitivity analysis, or uncertainty estimates.

The ToolBench result is mediated by both a GPT-4o-mini API simulator and a GPT-4.1 outcome judge rather than real API execution. This can reward compatibility with the simulator or judge and limits how strongly the results establish robust real-world tool use.

The SQuAD comparison imports baseline values from prior work rather than clearly rerunning all methods under the same implementation and judging pipeline. The paper should establish exact comparability and report variance; the small differences in some CPT settings are otherwise difficult to interpret.

The study does not measure collateral effects on general language ability, previously learned knowledge, calibration, or source-domain skills after adding a full-model vector. Such retention tests are important for a method framed as continual adaptation. Practical accounting should also include the storage and application cost of full-parameter vectors and the amortized source-RL cost.

Reproducibility is aided by the detailed appendix, but no code, generated training data, trained checkpoints or skill vectors, random seeds, or deterministic evaluation protocol are identified. Reproducing the results would therefore remain expensive and partially underspecified.

Overall, the empirical method and consistent improvements support a Findings-level contribution, but the unsupported theoretical language, missing causal controls, restricted model/domain coverage, and evaluation uncertainty prevent a main-conference recommendation in the present form.
